items.evidence: Pointers in C are variables that store the memory addresses of other variables.
items.note: The student correctly defines a pointer as a variable storing a memory address.

items.evidence: You can initialize a pointer using the address-of operator to reference an existing variable.
items.note: The student explains that the address-of operator retrieves a variable's location.

items.evidence: To access or modify the value stored at that memory location, you use the dereference operator.
items.note: The student explains that dereferencing accesses the value at the stored address.

items.evidence: Declaring a pointer only creates the pointer variable itself; it does not allocate memory for the data it points to
items.note: The student notes that memory is not automatically allocated for the data, but misses mentioning garbage addresses.

items.evidence: Pointer arithmetic is also type-aware, meaning incrementing a pointer advances it by the size of its data type in bytes.
items.note: The student correctly explains that pointer arithmetic scales by the byte size of the data type.
The student did not mention NULL pointers at all.
The student did not discuss pass-by-reference or function arguments.

target_reason: Understanding NULL pointers is essential for safely managing and checking pointer validity.
target_focus: what a pointer contains when it does not point anywhere
